Keeping my response simple and without going into boring legal procedure:
Assuming Q means 'post filing' with a court, the indictment cannot just disappear. (Hahaha, although many of us know of some that seem to have done just that) If the rules are followed, there can be an action by the prosecutor to withdraw one or all of the counts (charges) contained in the indictment. That can occur without the person named as the defendant in the indictment ever appearing in court. If the prosecutor withdraws all of the counts in the indictment, this is one way - to use the informal expression - the indictment has been pulled.

Also, an arraignment on an indictment can be removed from the court's calendar by request of the prosecutor and consent of the court - thereby postponing the unsealing of the indictment... excessive delay could lead to the indictment getting thrown out, depending on the charges and statute of limitations issues, etc. etc. a lot of legal rules and wrangling are available to clever people.. all of which creates another 'round about way of pulling the indictment.

A judge may direct secrecy until the defendant is in custody - pretty standard stuff. I've never seen a judge not direct secrecy on a sealed indictment until after the defendant is in custody. Many of them would run if they aren't in custody. The "or has been released pending trial" assumes that if the person is in custody after being charged the indictment could stay sealed, I've never seen that. maybe it happens, but it is not common practice. Once the person is arraigned, the indictment is unsealed and the charges SHOULD then public information. Lower and mid-level public officials deal with this issue often - it's the big and powerful who get the protection from public scrutiny.

legal procedure is whacky and there is a way to do just about anything if the players are willing and if no proceedings have occurred in open court post arraignment. One odd thing about sealed indictments, they almost always hold the arraignments on them during a time when no one is around - meaning when there is no public or press in the courtroom. It leaves the players lots of wiggle room. In all fairness, I must note that sometimes it is truly done to protect the victims, such as children.
